A.summary: Every GPU problem shows up first as a Linux symptom: a slow node, a missing device, a stuck process. You need a fixed order of checks and a clear picture of how a GPU reaches a container.
ideas: USE method: for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, GPU) check utilization, saturation and errors. It turns 'the node is slow' into a checklist.
Low GPU utilization usually means the GPU is waiting: for data loading, host-to-device copies, CPU work or communication. Look at the CPU side before blaming the GPU.

A GPU reaches a container through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit: device nodes (/dev/nvidia*), host driver libraries and cgroup device rules are injected at start. CDI (Container Device Interface) is the newer, declarative way to describe them.
The kernel module and the user-space driver libraries must be the same version. 'Driver/library version mismatch' means one was upgraded without the other being reloaded.
Persistence mode (nvidia-persistenced) keeps the driver initialised, so the first CUDA call doesn't pay a multi-second start-up cost.
pitfalls: Reading 'free' memory instead of 'available'
Upgrading the driver on a node without draining it first
Assuming the WSL2 virtual NIC behaves like a real one (use a VM for NIC and RDMA work)
A.probe: A node is slow: what do you run first, and what does each command rule out? Walk from kubectl apply to a GPU visible inside the pod.

B.summary: GPU health is read from three places: kernel XID errors, ECC and row-remapping counters, and active diagnostics (DCGM, burn-in). Fleets combine passive monitoring with scheduled active tests.
ideas: XID errors are the driver's error codes in the kernel log (NVRM: Xid ...). Some point to the application (13, 31, 43), some to memory (48, 63, 64, 92, 94, 95), NVLink (74), the PCIe bus (79) or GPU firmware (119, 120).
ECC: single-bit errors are corrected; double-bit errors are not. Modern data-center GPUs replace bad memory rows with row remapping, which takes effect after a GPU reset.

DCGM diagnostic levels: r1 is a seconds-long sanity check, r2 adds PCIe/NVLink and memory tests, r3 adds stress, power, bandwidth and NCCL plugins, r4 adds long memory tests. Use r1 at job start and r3 at acceptance.
Burn-in means hours of load while logging temperature, power, clocks and clock-event (throttle) reasons. Weak GPUs show up as clocks below their peers, not only as crashes.
Remediation ladder: reset the GPU, reboot the node, then RMA. Automation needs a circuit breaker so a fleet-wide event doesn't drain the whole cluster.
pitfalls: Alerting on utilization instead of errors
Treating XID 63 (informational) like XID 79 (critical)
Remediating automatically with no limit on how many nodes can be drained at once
B.probe: XID 79 appears in dmesg: what does it mean and what do you do? What does DCGM r3 add over r2?

C.summary: Performance depends on where things sit: which CPU socket, which PCIe switch, which NIC. Topology decides whether data takes the short path or crosses the system.
ideas: Read nvidia-smi topo -m: PIX/PXB means the same PCIe switch tree, PHB the same host bridge, NODE the same NUMA node, SYS crosses CPU sockets (slowest), NV# means NVLink.
NUMA: a GPU and its NIC belong to one CPU socket. A process or buffer on the other socket makes every copy cross the inter-socket link.
PCIe links can train down silently (x16 to x8, Gen5 to Gen3). Compare LnkCap with LnkSta under load and check AER error counters.
GPUDirect RDMA lets a NIC read and write GPU memory directly. It needs the GPU and NIC under the same root complex (ideally the same switch), IOMMU off or in pass-through, and the peer-memory module.
In HGX systems, eight GPUs connect through NVSwitch for all-to-all NVLink bandwidth inside the node; the NICs (usually one per GPU) carry traffic between nodes.
pitfalls: Checking PCIe link speed while the GPU is idle (it downclocks)
Binding ranks to the wrong NUMA node
Expecting cloud VMs to expose every PCIe detail that bare metal does
C.probe: Draw an 8-GPU HGX node. A GPU shows half the expected PCIe bandwidth: what do you check?

D.summary: The BMC is a small independent computer on the server board. It lets you see and control the machine when the OS is down, which is most of early bring-up.
ideas: The BMC has its own network port and power. It reports sensors (temperature, fans, power supplies), keeps the System Event Log (SEL), gives a serial console and can power-cycle the host.
IPMI is the older binary protocol. Redfish is HTTPS + JSON with a published schema, sessions and eventing, which is why large fleets automate with it.
Redfish tree: /redfish/v1/Systems (the host), Chassis (thermal, power), Managers (the BMC), UpdateService (firmware), with LogServices for event logs.
Fleet hygiene: one golden BIOS/firmware baseline per platform, drift detection over Redfish, staged remediation in maintenance windows.
OCP's diagnostic output format standardises test results across vendors, the kind of detail hyperscaler hardware teams care about.
pitfalls: Leaving default BMC credentials or exposing BMCs on a routable network
Assuming attribute names are the same across server vendors
Reading GPU temperatures without inlet temperatures (cooling vs workload)
D.probe: IPMI vs Redfish: what changed and why? Rack 14 has hot GPUs: how do you prove it is cooling and not workload?

E.summary: Training moves huge buffers between GPUs every step. RDMA fabrics (InfiniBand, RoCE, AWS EFA) do it without CPU copies; their design and congestion control decide how well jobs scale.
ideas: RDMA lets a NIC read or write remote memory directly. Core objects: queue pairs (QP), registered memory regions (MR), protection domains (PD) and completion queues (CQ).
InfiniBand uses credit-based, lossless link-level flow control and a subnet manager. RoCEv2 runs RDMA over UDP (port 4791) on Ethernet and relies on PFC, ECN and DCQCN to avoid loss and congestion.
AWS EFA exposes its SRD transport through libfabric; NCCL reaches it through the aws-ofi-nccl plugin. Security groups must allow all traffic to and from themselves.
Rail-optimised networks connect NIC k of every node to the same leaf switches, so same-rank traffic stays one hop away; cross-rail traffic uses NVLink inside the node.
Health signals: symbol errors, link-downed counts, receive errors, transmit discards and wait counters. Rising counters on one link point to a cable, transceiver or port.
pitfalls: Comparing Soft-RoCE numbers with real NIC numbers (it's a concept lab)
NCCL silently falling back to TCP sockets
Ignoring oversubscription when sizing spine switches
E.probe: Explain RDMA to a cloud engineer in 60 seconds. NCCL falls back to sockets on an EFA cluster: first three checks?

F.summary: NCCL is the library that moves data between GPUs. Its benchmark numbers are the clearest health signal for a training cluster, if you know how to read them.
ideas: Collectives: all-reduce (sum gradients across ranks), all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all (expert parallelism), broadcast.
algbw = bytes / time. busbw corrects for the algorithm so it is comparable to link bandwidth whatever the rank count: all-reduce x 2(n-1)/n, all-gather and reduce-scatter x (n-1)/n.
Ring algorithms suit large messages; tree algorithms cut latency at scale. NCCL picks automatically, and NCCL_ALGO lets you compare.
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows which transport and NIC it chose (NVLink, P2P, NET/IB, NET/OFI for EFA, Socket). Always check it before trusting a number.
Collectives move at the speed of the slowest rank: one straggler slows everyone, one dead rank hangs everyone until a timeout fires.
pitfalls: Quoting small-message busbw as the cluster's bandwidth
Benchmarking without checking the transport in NCCL_DEBUG
No timeout, so a dead rank hangs a job for hours
F.probe: algbw vs busbw: why does busbw exist? busbw drops going from 2 to 4 nodes: where do you look?

G.summary: Most large training clusters run Slurm; many companies run Kubernetes or both. You need to operate Slurm, keep bad nodes out of the queue and know how servers become nodes in the first place.
ideas: Slurm: slurmctld (controller), slurmd (per node), partitions, sbatch/srun/squeue/sacct. GPUs are generic resources (GRES) declared in gres.conf.
With cgroup ConstrainDevices a job sees only its allocated GPUs (exposed through CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
Prolog, epilog and Node Health Check (NHC) drain unhealthy nodes before jobs land on them.
Pyxis + Enroot let Slurm jobs run containers unprivileged (srun --container-image).
Provisioning: BMC power-on, PXE/iPXE boot, image, config management, burn-in, then join the scheduler. Tools: Warewulf, MAAS, Ironic, Metal3, Tinkerbell.
pitfalls: gres.conf and the NodeName line disagreeing on GPU count
Health checks that only run at boot
Picking Slurm vs Kubernetes on taste instead of on users, tenancy and operations
G.probe: How does Slurm keep one job's GPUs invisible to another? A customer asks Slurm or Kubernetes for training: how do you answer?

H.summary: On Kubernetes, GPUs arrive through operators and device APIs. The hard parts are sharing GPUs, scheduling whole jobs at once, giving pods RDMA, and remediating bad nodes safely.
ideas: The GPU Operator installs driver (optional), container toolkit, device plugin, GPU feature discovery, DCGM exporter and validators as DaemonSets.
The device plugin advertises a count (nvidia.com/gpu). Dynamic Resource Allocation (GA since Kubernetes v1.34) lets claims select devices by attributes and handle groups such as NVLink domains.
Sharing: time-slicing (no isolation), MPS (concurrent kernels, limited isolation), MIG (hardware partitions of memory and compute on A100/H100-class GPUs).
Distributed jobs need gang scheduling: start all pods or none. Kueue provides quota, borrowing and all-or-nothing admission (API v1beta2 since v0.20); KAI Scheduler and Volcano are alternatives.
The Network Operator plus Multus and an RDMA device plugin give pods a secondary RDMA interface; Node Problem Detector plus a remediator handle bad nodes.
pitfalls: Time-slicing for tenants that need isolation
Partial gang starts that hold GPUs and deadlock the queue
Remediation without a maxUnhealthy limit
H.probe: What does the GPU Operator install, and in what order? Two teams share 256 GPUs: how do you enforce quota and avoid deadlock?

I.summary: Customers rent GPUs from clouds. Knowing what each cloud really gives you (NICs per GPU, fabric, placement, quotas, storage) is what separates a cloud-aware architect from a hardware specialist.
ideas: The same GPU can perform differently across clouds: NIC count and speed per GPU, fabric type and NCCL plugin, rail design and placement all matter.
Capacity is a project in itself: quotas, capacity reservations or blocks, placement groups and per-zone limits come before any Terraform.
Storage tiers: object store (source of truth), local NVMe (cache), parallel file system (shared high throughput). Model load and checkpoint time are storage problems.
Large rollouts go in waves with entry and exit criteria, a spare pool and a rollback plan.
pitfalls: Requesting the Spot quota when you launch On-Demand (they are separate)
Spreading one training job across zones
Forgetting checkpoint write time when sizing storage
I.probe: Why do two clouds with the same GPU give different all-reduce numbers? You have four weeks to bring up 1,024 GPUs: what is your plan?

J.summary: Observability for GPU fleets means the right metrics, the right alerts and the ability to turn failure data into decisions.
ideas: dcgm-exporter publishes DCGM fields to Prometheus: utilization, memory, power, temperature, XID errors, NVLink counters and profiling metrics (SM activity, tensor-core activity).
Utilization is not efficiency. A GPU can show 100% 'utilization' while doing little useful work; profiling metrics and MFU tell the truth.
Alert on XID errors, uncorrectable ECC and row-remap failures, missing GPUs, throttling and NVLink errors.
Fleet metrics: failures per 1,000 GPU-days, mean time between interruptions, time to repair, cohorted by rack, firmware, driver and hardware batch.
pitfalls: Dashboards with no alert rules
Not mapping GPU metrics to jobs or tenants
Reporting averages that hide one bad rack
J.probe: Which three GPU metrics do you alert on, and why not utilization alone? How do you tell a bad GPU batch from a bad rack?

K.summary: You don't need to train models, but you must do the arithmetic and speak the workload's language: memory, compute, parallelism and serving metrics.
ideas: Training memory with mixed precision and Adam is about 16 bytes per parameter before activations: a 70B model needs about 1.1 TB of state.
KV cache per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes. It grows with context and concurrency and usually sets the serving batch size.
Training compute is about 6 x parameters x tokens FLOPs. MFU (model FLOPs utilisation) = achieved / peak; 35-50% is typical for well-tuned large jobs.
Parallelism: data parallel / FSDP shards state, tensor parallel splits layers (needs NVLink), pipeline parallel splits stages, expert parallel uses all-to-all.
Serving metrics: time to first token (prefill), inter-token latency (decode), throughput. Disaggregated serving puts prefill and decode on separate GPUs and moves the KV cache over the fabric.
pitfalls: Tensor parallelism across PCIe-only GPUs
Ignoring checkpoint cost when estimating useful training time
Quoting tokens/s without the batch size and context length
K.probe: Can a 70B model train on one 8x80 GB node? Show the maths. MFU is 25%: where do you look?

L.summary: The capstone turns 48 labs into one story you can tell in ten minutes, backed by a public repository.
ideas: One command builds, validates and tears down a cluster and writes a dated report against a criteria file.
Injected failures prove the kit works: a simulated XID, EFA disabled, wrong NUMA binding, a power-capped straggler.
The README sells it: architecture diagram, results, cost per run, and what changes at 2,000 GPUs.
Public proof (posts, pull requests, a talk) shows you can communicate, which the posting stresses as much as skill.
pitfalls: A repo that only works on your laptop
Results with no thresholds or explanation
Leaving cloud resources running after the demo
L.probe: Walk me through your validation kit: what it checks, what it caught and what a run costs.
